mcqs.question: Why are retrieval-stage models in a multi-stage pipeline deliberately simpler than ranking-stage models?
options: Because the whole request shares one latency SLA split across stages, so retrieval's slice of the budget hard-constrains how much compute its model can spend, regardless of what would be most accurate in isolation
Because retrieval models are trained on less data than ranking models by convention
Because ranking models are always more accurate than retrieval models on any metric
Because retrieval only ever runs on cached results and never needs a model at all
mcqs.explanation: The constraint is architectural, not a training-data or accuracy preference — each stage only gets a fraction of the total latency budget, and retrieval's slice is small because it has to scan the largest candidate pool. It's not about relative accuracy in the abstract, and retrieval very much uses a model (just a cheaper one), not pure caching.

mcqs.question: In a common multi-region ML serving compromise, why is training kept centralized while inference is replicated across regions?
options: Because training requires a physical data center in every region by law

Because inference is latency-sensitive to user proximity while training is not, so replicating the trained artifact for low-latency serving captures the benefit without paying the cost of distributing the training process itself
Because model artifacts cannot be copied between regions
Because centralizing training eliminates the need for a model registry
mcqs.explanation: The split follows directly from which part of the system actually needs to be geographically close to users — inference latency matters per-request, training does not, since it happens offline ahead of time. There's no such legal requirement, model artifacts are routinely replicated across regions, and a registry is still needed regardless of where training happens.

mcqs.question: What specific problem does a feature store solve that a single centralized feature definition alone wouldn't?
options: It provides two consistent read paths (batch for training, low-latency online for serving) derived from the same feature definitions, preventing train/serve skew from features being computed differently in each path
It guarantees the model architecture never needs to change
It removes the need for a separate model registry
It eliminates the need for any online inference entirely
mcqs.explanation: The specific value of a feature store is having both a batch and an online path draw from the same underlying feature logic, so training and serving see the same feature values computed the same way — directly preventing train/serve skew. It doesn't touch model architecture decisions, doesn't replace a model registry, and doesn't eliminate the need for online inference where that's required.

mcqs.question: Why do production ML systems monitor feature and prediction drift directly, rather than waiting for a business metric like revenue to visibly move?
options: Business metrics move instantly with any model degradation, so drift monitoring is redundant
Drift monitoring is only useful for fraud detection systems specifically

A model's accuracy can decay as the underlying data distribution shifts well before that decay is visible in a lagging business metric, so drift alerts catch degradation earlier, while there's still time to retrain
Feature drift and prediction drift are the same measurement, so tracking both is unnecessary
mcqs.explanation: Business metrics are often lagging and noisy, so real degradation can already be underway before it's visible there — drift monitoring gives an earlier, more direct signal tied to the model's actual inputs and outputs. Business metrics don't move instantly with model issues, drift monitoring is broadly useful (not fraud-specific), and feature drift and prediction drift are distinct signals worth tracking separately.

mcqs.question: A model shows strong offline evaluation metrics before launch. Why isn't that sufficient proof it will perform the same in production?
options: Offline evaluation always uses the exact same code path as production serving, so there's nothing left to verify
Offline metrics are computed on a different model than the one deployed

The serving path computes features independently from the training pipeline, and any difference between the two (a different time window, null-handling, a stale cache) means the model sees different inputs live than it was ever evaluated against
Offline evaluation metrics are randomly generated and carry no real signal
mcqs.explanation: Offline metrics only reflect the training pipeline's feature computation; if the serving path computes even one feature differently, production inputs diverge from what was evaluated, and a strong offline score says nothing about that specific gap. Offline and serving paths are frequently different code, offline evaluation does use the actual candidate model, and its metrics are meaningful, just insufficient alone.
